title: Vertex AI Embeddings In Iteration One
text: The first version of this project uses Vertex AI to generate dense vector embeddings for every document chunk. Each chunk is embedded with the RETRIEVAL_DOCUMENT task type so the model optimizes the vector for search over a document corpus. User questions are embedded separately with the RETRIEVAL_QUERY task type, which helps narrow the semantic gap between questions and answers. This design keeps the logic simple while still using a production-grade Google Cloud embedding service.

title: Cloud Storage As The System Of Record
text: Cloud Storage is the easiest place to keep both the raw source documents and the generated artifacts for this interview project. The source dataset can live in a bucket as JSONL files, and the output index can also be uploaded after ingestion finishes. That gives the project a clean separation between local development and durable storage. In a follow-up iteration, the same bucket can also hold batch input files, chunk exports, or evaluation datasets.

title: Why Retrieval Stays Local At First
text: Iteration one deliberately keeps retrieval local, even though the project is built around Google Cloud services. A tiny dataset does not need approximate nearest neighbor infrastructure, private endpoints, or index deployment workflows. Local cosine similarity over a JSON file is enough to prove that embeddings are created correctly, chunks are ranked correctly, and sources are returned clearly. This choice reduces cost, reduces setup time, and makes the repository much easier to understand in an interview setting. Once the retrieval flow works end to end, the local index can be replaced by Vertex AI Vector Search with minimal conceptual changes.

title: The Upgrade Path To Vertex AI Vector Search
text: The second iteration should replace the local JSON index with Vertex AI Vector Search. At that point, the chunking code and embedding flow can stay mostly the same, but the indexed vectors should be uploaded into a managed vector index. That upgrade matters when the dataset grows, when latency targets get tighter, or when the project needs operational features such as managed endpoints and approximate nearest neighbor retrieval. The main reason to postpone this step is that it adds more setup, more waiting time during index deployment, and more moving parts than a first interview demo really needs.

title: What The Demo Should Show
text: A good interview demo should show the full retrieval pipeline and not just a diagram. The repo should include a small but coherent dataset, a repeatable ingestion command, a saved index artifact, and a query command that prints the top matching chunks with scores and source references. That makes it easy to explain the end-to-end story: documents are chunked, embedded, indexed, retrieved, and traced back to their origin. Even without answer generation, that is already enough to demonstrate the core of a RAG system.

title: How A Future Cloud Run API Would Fit
text: A later version of the project can expose retrieval through a small Cloud Run service. The API could accept a user question, generate a query embedding with Vertex AI, retrieve the top chunks, and optionally pass those chunks into a Gemini prompt for answer generation. Cloud Run is a good fit because it keeps the service simple, container-based, and easy to deploy from source control. For the first iteration, however, a command line interface is enough because the main goal is validating the retrieval workflow rather than production hosting.

title: What To Measure After The First Demo
text: Once the first demo works, the next useful step is adding lightweight evaluation. The project can define a short list of test questions and the chunk ids that should appear in the top results. That makes it possible to measure recall at k, inspect bad matches, and compare changes in chunking or embedding settings. Even simple offline evaluation makes the project feel much more like an engineering system than a one-off script.
